title: Nature's prescription
hookLine: as doctors prescribe cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss; take it like medicine (Meditations 5.8)

lines: YOU DON'T ARGUE WITH A PRESCRIPTION.
cards: Physical therapy hurts. The stretch you're told to hold for thirty seconds feels like three minutes. The exercise for your knee is boring and sore.
And yet people do it, more or less cheerfully, because someone they trust wrote it down and said: this will help. You don't argue with a prescription the way you argue with bad luck.
Marcus Aurelius noticed that difference, and in book five, entry eight, he tried to move the hard things in his life from one column to the other.

teach.b: People say, Marcus writes, Asclepius prescribed this man horseback riding, or cold baths, or walking barefoot.
Asclepius was the Greek god of healing, and in Marcus's world people spoke of his prescriptions the way we speak of a doctor's orders.
In the same way, he says, the nature of the whole prescribed for this person an illness, or a disability, or a loss. The word for prescribed is the same.

In his view the event isn't random; it's fitted to you, the way a prescription is written for one patient. He gives two reasons to accept it. One: it happened to you, it was assigned to you, it's woven into your own life.

teach.h: YOURS, AND PART OF THE WHOLE.
teach.b: Two: it serves the health of the whole universe, which he believed was one living order. You don't have to share his belief about the cosmos to feel the force of the first reason. This is your life, and this is in it.
So, he says, accept what happens the way you accept what the doctor orders.
Many prescriptions are bitter, and we welcome them anyway, hoping for health. You can't always choose whether hard things come.
But you can choose their column: bad luck, to be resented, or medicine, to be taken. Marcus isn't saying it doesn't taste bitter. He's saying bitter isn't the same as wrong.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes reframe a hardship as in Meditations 5.8, accepting it as a doctor's order rather than resenting it only as bad luck.

o: a list of old Roman rules for eating and living well
a natural cure, like herbs, that heals any illness
hard things taken as medicine, bitter but meant for health

s: Marcus says hard things don't really hurt
he grants they're bitter, like many prescriptions, and says take them anyway.
Marcus gives two reasons to accept what happens
it's assigned to your life, and it serves the health of the whole.
Marcus uses the same word, prescribed, for the doctor and for nature
Asclepius prescribed a cold bath; the nature of the whole prescribed an illness.

games.q: an injury means three months off from running, which you love. what fits Meditations 5.8?
o: treat it as a prescription, and ask what it's for.
run anyway, to prove you can.
decide the universe is against you.
games.why: Marcus takes hardship the way we take a doctor's orders: bitter, but accepted, hoping for health.

practice: Bring to mind one hard thing in your life right now, an ache, a limit, a loss, a difficult person, and notice which column it's been in.

Just for these breaths, picture it on a prescription pad with your name at the top, and ask Marcus's first question: is this part of my own life, assigned to me? Then take it, the way you'd take a bitter pill the doctor ordered.

wordCard.voice: Nature's prescription. Marcus says as a doctor prescribes cold baths, nature prescribes illness or loss: take it as medicine, bitter but meant for health. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Asclepius, god of healing, whose prescriptions Marcus compares to what nature assigns.

carryVoice: Your line: the prescription. Bitter isn't the same as wrong. Take good care.
